It’s been a while since I’ve done any handle pulling but what a joy it is to be back at it, although in this never-ending heatwave it’s a more finicky process than it normally is. Together with being a process that’s all about your control in terms of how you handle the clay, it’s also a process that’s incredibly sensitive to temperature and the condition of the clay itself.   For instance, if you attached handles when the cup is too soft, the walls of the vessel will distort and you’ll very easily destroy the mug. If the cup is too hard, then the likelihood that the handle cracks as it dries is far higher, as there’s a greater disparity in the levels of moisture in the two contrasting parts.   Of course, both of those facts are exacerbated if the handle lengths/blanks you’re creating are either too soft or too firm, for example if the blacks are too soft, then it can be practically impossible to form them further without them ripping of sagging and losing their shapes. At the same time, if they’re too hard, which can happen if you leave the blanks exposed for too long, or if you leave them on a wooden surface that wicks out moisture from one side of them, you’ll have a troublesome time getting them to have a smooth, flowing shape, as firm clay is stubborn and needs more pressure and water, which again, raises the chances that you’ll rip the handle off.   Now, both of those facts can be exacerbated if the mug itself is too soft or too dry, which means in total you’re trying to monitor so many variables so that you’re pulling the handles in that perfect moment, whilst attaching them to a cup that’s precisely the right-level of leather hard.    All of that is of course information you can only really learn through practice and it’s why this technique can be punishing at the beginning as you have to ruin pots in order to learn the materials limits. Equally, potters trying this for the first time will often be able to make pretty decent pots, which makes it feel extremely disappointing when you attach scruffy handles onto them. This is why I think it’s often a skill that’s quickly abandoned but you’ve just got to get through those teething pains!   #pottery #ceramics #satisfying #handmade #asmr

pricing my work is truly my LEAST favourite thing 😭  especially after trying to look closer at the numbers behind my small ceramic business. i’m trying to map out the potential 1, 3, and 5 year revenue and expense projections to see if investing in a kiln and building this business actually makes any sense. at my current $30-$65 price point, i’m losing money selling my work and cannot justify a kiln. i’ve made the terrifying decision to raise my prices by 25-30%. the money will go towards expanding production (investing. in a kiln & shelving), upgrading my website, expanding to ship to the US, and finally, offering private lessons and workshops.  with the price increase, I will still need to survive 6 months - 1 year without a livable wage / making profit. i’ll be focusing on my higher-margin petal bowls and bring in some more affordable $25 products like spoon rests and trinket dishes to keep things as accessible as possible. my mugs are not viable as they take me 2hrs each, but i’m going to keep making them for now and hope i can speed it up. no more lidded jars outside of speciality collections as the margins are too low.  i’m also going to try to secure 1-2 freelance social media clients to provide me with some supplement income as a buffer. this is the behind the scenes of small ceramics business’ that you normally don’t see, because it’s not nearly as cute or fun as the pots themselves. #potterybusiness #ceramics #smallbusiness #priceincrease #handmadeceramics
